mcqs.explain: Total binding energy = (binding energy per nucleon) × A. For lead-208: 7.9 MeV × 208 = 1.6 × 10³ MeV; for iron-56: 8.8 MeV × 56 = 4.9 × 10² MeV; the ratio is 3.3. Because E_b/A is roughly constant, the total E_b is roughly proportional to A, even though the per-nucleon value is slightly lower for lead.
mcqs.working: Total binding energy E_b = (E_b/A) × A. Lead-208: 7.9 MeV × 208 = 1643 MeV ≈ 1.6 × 10³ MeV. Iron-56: 8.8 MeV × 56 = 492.8 MeV ≈ 4.9 × 10² MeV. Ratio = 1643/492.8 = 3.33 ≈ 3.3. (If E_b grew as A², the ratio would be (208/56)² = 13.8 ≈ 14.)
rationales: Total binding energy = (binding energy per nucleon) × A. For lead-208: 7.9 MeV × 208 = 1.6 × 10³ MeV; for iron-56: 8.8 MeV × 56 = 4.9 × 10² MeV; the ratio is 3.3. Because E_b/A is roughly constant, the total E_b is roughly proportional to A, even though the per-nucleon value is slightly lower for lead.

A student who uses binding energy and binding energy per nucleon interchangeably picks this. Iron-56 has the larger value PER NUCLEON, but lead-208 has almost four times as many nucleons, so its total binding energy (about 1600 MeV) far exceeds iron-56's (about 490 MeV).

A student who assumes the strong force has a long range expects the number of attracting pairs, and so the total binding energy, to grow roughly as A², giving (208/56)² ≈ 14. The near-constant E_b/A shows the total grows in proportion to A, giving a ratio of only about 3.3: evidence that each nucleon is bound only to its near neighbours.

A student who thinks binding energy is energy stored in the nucleus picks this. 1.6 × 10³ MeV is the energy that would have to be SUPPLIED to separate all 208 nucleons; a reaction releases only the difference between the total binding energies of the products and the reactants.

mcqs.q: Thorium-228 decays by α emission to radium-224, which has an excited state 0.08 MeV above its ground state. The α particles emitted when radium-224 is formed in its ground state have kinetic energy 5.42 MeV. Ignoring the recoil of the radium nucleus, which statement about the α particles emitted when radium-224 is formed in its excited state is correct?
options: They have kinetic energy 5.50 MeV, as they carry the extra 0.08 MeV that the excited radium nucleus possesses.
They also have kinetic energy 5.42 MeV, because a given nuclide emits α particles of a single energy only.
They have kinetic energies anywhere between 5.34 MeV and 5.42 MeV, as the nucleus can be left with any energy up to 0.08 MeV.
They have kinetic energy 5.34 MeV, and a 0.08 MeV γ photon is emitted as the radium nucleus falls to its ground state.
mcqs.specStatementText: that the spectrum of alpha and gamma radiations provides evidence for discrete nuclear energy levels
mcqs.explain: The energy released in the decay is fixed. If the radium nucleus keeps 0.08 MeV as excitation energy, the α particle receives 5.42 − 0.08 = 5.34 MeV. The excited nucleus then drops to its ground state, emitting the 0.08 MeV as a γ photon: two discrete α energies and one discrete γ energy, as discrete nuclear energy levels require.
mcqs.working: Energy released is the same in every decay of thorium-228 to radium-224. Ground-state decay: E_α = 5.42 MeV (recoil ignored). Decay to the excited state: the daughter retains 0.08 MeV, so E_α = 5.42 − 0.08 = 5.34 MeV. The excited radium-224 nucleus then emits a γ photon of energy 0.08 MeV. (Measured values: α energies 5.423 MeV and 5.340 MeV; γ energy 0.084 MeV.)
rationales: A student who attaches the 'extra' excitation energy to the α particle adds 0.08 MeV. The energy released is fixed; energy kept by the daughter as excitation is NOT available to the α particle, so these α particles have 0.08 MeV LESS, not more.

A student who thinks each nuclide has a single α energy picks this. One nuclide can emit α particles of several discrete energies, one for each energy level of the daughter in which it can be left; the energy kept by the excited daughter reduces the α energy to 5.34 MeV.

A student who thinks nuclear energy is continuous picks this. The radium nucleus can be left only in its ground state or in the discrete excited state 0.08 MeV above it, so the α particles have only the two energies 5.42 MeV and 5.34 MeV, not a continuous range.

The energy released in the decay is fixed. If the radium nucleus keeps 0.08 MeV as excitation energy, the α particle receives 5.42 − 0.08 = 5.34 MeV. The excited nucleus then drops to its ground state, emitting the 0.08 MeV as a γ photon: two discrete α energies and one discrete γ energy, as discrete nuclear energy levels require.

mcqs.q: The α particles from a given decay to the daughter's ground state all have the same kinetic energy, whereas the β⁻ particles from a given decay have a continuous range of kinetic energies up to a maximum. Which statement correctly explains this difference?
options: α decay produces two bodies, so conservation of momentum fixes the α particle's share of the energy; β⁻ decay produces three, so the electron's share can vary.
Both kinds of particle leave the nucleus with a single energy, but β⁻ particles lose varying amounts of energy in collisions before they escape the source.
Every α decay of a nuclide releases exactly the same energy, but the energy released varies from one β⁻ decay to the next, so the electron's energy varies with it.
The β⁻ particle shares the released energy with a γ photon emitted at the same instant, whereas an α particle takes all of the energy.
mcqs.specStatementText: the continuous spectrum of beta decay as evidence for the neutrino
mcqs.explain: With two products, conservation of momentum and energy together fix how the released energy is divided, so every α particle has the same energy. With three products (daughter, electron and antineutrino) the energy can be divided in many ways, so the electron's energy varies from zero up to the maximum, and the antineutrino takes the rest.
rationales: With two products, conservation of momentum and energy together fix how the released energy is divided, so every α particle has the same energy. With three products (daughter, electron and antineutrino) the energy can be divided in many ways, so the electron's energy varies from zero up to the maximum, and the antineutrino takes the rest.

A student who looks for an ordinary cause of the spread picks this. The spread is present at emission, and α particles, being far more ionizing, would lose MORE energy in collisions than β⁻ particles, yet their spectrum is discrete. The continuous β⁻ spectrum needs a third particle.

A student who thinks nuclear energy levels are continuous picks this. The daughter nucleus of a β⁻ decay, like that of an α decay, can be left only in discrete energy states, so the energy released is the same in every decay; the variation lies in how it is shared with the antineutrino.

A student who takes the third particle to be a photon picks this. γ photons are emitted later, by an excited daughter nucleus, with discrete energies; they are not produced in every decay. The particle that shares the energy in every β⁻ decay is the antineutrino.

mcqs.q: A sample contains 8.0 × 10²⁰ nuclei of iodine-131, which has a half-life of 8.0 days. How many iodine-131 nuclei remain after 20 days?
mcqs.specStatementText: the decay constant λ and the radioactive decay law as given by N = N₀e^(−λt)
mcqs.explain: λ = ln 2/T½ = 0.693/8.0 days = 0.0866 day⁻¹. N = N₀e^(−λt) = 8.0 × 10²⁰ × e^(−0.0866 × 20) = 8.0 × 10²⁰ × e^(−1.73) = 8.0 × 10²⁰ × 0.177 = 1.4 × 10²⁰. This lies between the values for 2 half-lives (2.0 × 10²⁰) and 3 half-lives (1.0 × 10²⁰), as it should for 2.5 half-lives.
rationales: A student who divides by the number of half-lives gets 8.0 × 10²⁰/2.5 = 3.2 × 10²⁰. Each half-life halves the number, so 2.5 half-lives divide it by 2^2.5 = 5.66, not by 2.5.

λ = ln 2/T½ = 0.693/8.0 days = 0.0866 day⁻¹. N = N₀e^(−λt) = 8.0 × 10²⁰ × e^(−0.0866 × 20) = 8.0 × 10²⁰ × e^(−1.73) = 8.0 × 10²⁰ × 0.177 = 1.4 × 10²⁰. This lies between the values for 2 half-lives (2.0 × 10²⁰) and 3 half-lives (1.0 × 10²⁰), as it should for 2.5 half-lives.

A student who uses log₁₀ 2 = 0.301 instead of ln 2 = 0.693 gets λ = 0.0376 day⁻¹ and N = 8.0 × 10²⁰ × e^(−0.753) = 3.8 × 10²⁰. The decay law uses e, so its inverse is the natural logarithm: λ = ln 2/T½.

A student who rounds 20 days down to 2 whole half-lives (16 days) gets 8.0 × 10²⁰/4 = 2.0 × 10²⁰. The decay law N = N₀e^(−λt) applies at any time; after 2.5 half-lives the number is 8.0 × 10²⁰/2^2.5 = 1.4 × 10²⁰.

mcqs.q: The decay constant λ of a nuclide has the unit s⁻¹. Which statement about λ is correct?
options: The probability that a nucleus decays in a short time Δt is approximately λΔt, provided λΔt is much less than one.
The probability that a nucleus decays in a short time interval is approximately equal to λ, provided the interval is short.
The probability that a nucleus decays within a time t is exactly λt, however long the interval t may be.
The value of λ for a sample falls as the sample decays, because each surviving nucleus becomes less and less likely to decay.
mcqs.specStatementText: that the decay constant approximates the probability of decay in unit time only in the limit of sufficiently small λt
mcqs.explain: λ is the probability of decay per unit time, so for a short interval the probability of decay is about λΔt. The exact probability is 1 − e^(−λΔt), which equals λΔt only in the limit of small λΔt; for larger λΔt the approximation overestimates the probability.
rationales: λ is the probability of decay per unit time, so for a short interval the probability of decay is about λΔt. The exact probability is 1 − e^(−λΔt), which equals λΔt only in the limit of small λΔt; for larger λΔt the approximation overestimates the probability.

A student who takes λ itself to be a probability picks this. A probability has no unit, but λ has the unit s⁻¹: it is a probability PER UNIT TIME, and must be multiplied by a (short) time interval to give a probability.

A student who takes λ to be exactly the probability per unit time for all t picks this. For large t, λt exceeds 1, which no probability can do. The exact probability is 1 − e^(−λt); λt is a good approximation only when λt is much less than one.

A student who thinks a falling activity means each nucleus is less likely to decay picks this. λ is a constant of the nuclide: every undecayed nucleus has the same probability of decay per unit time at all times. The activity falls because there are fewer undecayed nuclei, not because λ changes.

mcqs.q: Technetium-99m, used in medical imaging, has a half-life of 6.0 h. What is its decay constant?
mcqs.specStatementText: the relationship between half-life and the decay constant as given by T½ = ln2/λ.
rationales: A student who uses λ = 1/T½ gets 1/(2.16 × 10⁴ s) = 4.6 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹. The half-life is the time for N to fall to N₀/2, so e^(−λT½) = ½ and λ = ln 2/T½; the factor 0.693 cannot be omitted.
A student who uses log₁₀ 2 = 0.301 instead of ln 2 = 0.693 gets 0.301/(2.16 × 10⁴ s) = 1.4 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹. The decay law is exponential in e, so it is the natural logarithm that appears: λ = ln 2/T½.

A student who divides ln 2 by 6.0 without converting the hours gets 0.12, which is λ in h⁻¹, not s⁻¹. λ has the unit of 1/time, so its value depends on the time unit: 0.12 h⁻¹ = 0.12/3600 s⁻¹ = 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹.

scopeNotes.statement: Nuclear masses will be expressed in kg, in MeV c⁻² and in (unified) atomic mass units u.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Nuclear masses appear in all three required units: in MeV c⁻² in q03 (proton, neutron and helium-4 nucleus) and in u, converted to kg with 1 u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, in q06 (radium-226 α decay), whose stem also gives 1 u = 931.5 MeV c⁻². Concept c03 defines the three units and their relationship.

scopeNotes.statement: An interpretation of binding energy curves is required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The binding energy curve is interpreted, with its values given in words and numbers because no graph can be shown: q04 asks which processes release energy from binding energies per nucleon spread across the curve, q05 calculates the energy released in deuterium–tritium fusion from binding energies per nucleon, and the HL item q25 interprets the flat part of the curve above A ≈ 60.

scopeNotes.statement: The weak nuclear force is not considered in this course.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: β⁻ and β⁺ decay are described only as a neutron changing into a proton (or a proton into a neutron) with the emission of a β particle and an antineutrino (or neutrino), balanced by conservation of nucleon number and charge. No item, concept, misconception or rationale refers to the weak nuclear force, to quarks or to exchange particles.

scopeNotes.statement: The weak nuclear force is not considered in this course.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Neutrinos and antineutrinos are described only by their charge, very small mass and very rare interaction with matter, and by the decays in which they are emitted (q11, q12, q13, q27); the interaction responsible for β decay is not named or discussed.

scopeNotes.statement: Real-life contexts for this topic should include the choice of isotope in medical use, leaks in underground pipes, thickness of materials, and radioactive dating based on the penetration of the decay particle and half-life.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: All four required contexts appear: choice of isotope in medical use (q14, technetium-99m, with γ penetration and the 6.0 h half-life), leaks in underground pipes (q15, sodium-24 detected through 1 m of soil), thickness of materials (q16, a β⁻ source for paper) and radioactive dating (q21 with a whole number of half-lives at SL, q28 over an arbitrary interval at HL). Each is reasoned from the penetration of the radiation, the half-life, or both.

scopeNotes.statement: The determination of the half-life of a nuclide is required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The half-life of a nuclide is determined from background-corrected count rates in q19 (three halvings in 120 min) and, at HL, from the gradient of a graph of ln(corrected count rate) against time in q32.

scopeNotes.statement: An application of the radioactive decay equations for arbitrary time intervals is required for additional higher level.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every SL (both-tier) item that calculates or states how much of a sample or its activity remains uses a whole number of half-lives: q09 (one further half-life after two), q18 (one and two), q19 (three), q20 (five), q21 (three) and q22 (three). Decay over an arbitrary time interval, using N = N₀e^(−λt), appears only in the HL items q28, q29 and q44.

scopeNotes.statement: An application of the radioactive decay equations for arbitrary time intervals is required for additional higher level.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The decay equations are applied to arbitrary time intervals at HL: q28 finds the age of bone whose activity has fallen to 23% (about 2.1 half-lives) and q29 finds the probability of decay in 5.0 s from 1 − e^(−λt) and q44 finds the number of iodine-131 nuclei remaining after 2.5 half-lives (20 days with T½ = 8.0 days).
